newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh unions warn of protests over unpaid wages.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh unions warn of protests over unpaid wages.

text.p: A Kazakh trade union leader said on Monday that massive protests could sweep the Central Asian state if the government did not take urgent steps to reduce a spiralling backlog of unpaid wages.

"Separate and spontaneous actions of protest over huge salary arrears have already taken place in some parts of the country," Leonid Solomin, head of the Kazakh Free Trade Unions Confederation, told Reuters in the capital Almaty.

He said 254 miners at the Achisaysky non-ferrous metals plant in Kentau, southern Kazakhstan, had occupied a set of administrative buildings since January 15, demanding unpaid salaries of 40 million tenge (about $500,000).

"Many miners in Kentau have not been paid for eight months, and some of them for more than two years. They have been driven to despair and even hunger because they have no money to buy bread," Solomin said.

At the weekend, Kazakh state television reported that school teachers in the northern Semipalatinsk region, unpaid for several months, planned to start an open-ended strike on Thursday if the government failed to pay their salaries.

Solomin said according to his estimates, unpaid salaries in the former Soviet republic amounted to 49 billion tenge (about $646 million). Debts to the state pension fund totalled 35 billion tenge (about $461 million), he said.
"Protests may become more numerous and organised if the authorities do not take urgent steps to improve the situation," he said.
There has been remarkably little protest from the republic's 16.9 million population despite severe economic hardship since independence in 1991.
But clearly concerned by the payments crisis, Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev last week told government and regional officials to reduce wage arrears by April 1 or face the sack.
Foreign exchange dealers in Almaty warned that any quick payment of salary and pension arrears could quicken inflation.
"This could lead to a shortage of dollars, which could cause the tenge to fall in value," said one dealer.
Kazakhstan, rich in oil and gas, is committed to slowing inflation under tough market economic reforms sponsored by the International Monetary Fund.
